title: VLANs: Native VLAN on a Router and Layer 3 Switching
summary: Two ways to configure the native VLAN on a router, what a dot1Q tag looks like in a Wireshark capture, and the third method of inter-VLAN routing — SVIs and routed ports on a multilayer switch.

sections.title: The native VLAN on a router

content.body:
Best practice is to set the native VLAN to an **unused VLAN**, because the native VLAN feature carries some security risks. But the feature does have one benefit: because native-VLAN frames are **not tagged**, each frame is 4 bytes smaller, so the device can push more frames per second.

If you do want to use it in a router-on-a-stick design, there are **two** ways to configure the native VLAN on the router — each is a complete solution:

**Option 1 — `native` keyword on a sub-interface**

```
R1(config)# interface g0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 10 native
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.1.62 255.255.255.192
```

The router now behaves like a switch does for the native VLAN: untagged frames arriving are assumed to be VLAN 10, and frames leaving this sub-interface are sent untagged.

**Option 2 — no sub-interface at all**

```
R1(config)# no interface g0/0.10
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.62 255.255.255.192
```

Configure the native VLAN's IP address directly on the **physical** interface. The `encapsulation dot1q` command is not needed. The other VLANs keep using their own sub-interfaces as normal.

sections.title: Seeing the dot1Q tag in Wireshark

content.body:
Capture the link between SW2 and R1 while a PC in VLAN 20 (`192.168.1.65`) pings a PC in VLAN 10 (`192.168.1.1`), with VLAN 10 configured as the native VLAN on both devices.

**ICMP echo request, SW2 → R1 (VLAN 20 — tagged):**

- `Type: 802.1Q Virtual LAN` with hexadecimal value **0x8100** — this is the **TPID**, sitting exactly where the Type field normally goes, right after the source MAC.
- **PCP** = 0, so no special priority.
- **DEI** = 0, so the frame is not drop-eligible during congestion.
- **VLAN ID** = 20, as expected.
- Then the *real* Type field, showing that an IPv4 packet is encapsulated.

**The same echo request, R1 → SW2 (VLAN 10 — native):**

Identical Layer 3 packet, new Ethernet header — but **no dot1Q tag at all**. Both R1 and SW2 understand that untagged frames on this trunk belong to VLAN 10, so there is no need to tag them. The request travels untagged all the way to the destination; when the reply comes back, it stays untagged until R1, which then tags it as VLAN 20.

Up to now every switch in this course has been a **Layer 2 switch** — not Layer 3 aware, caring only about MAC addresses. Many modern switches are also Layer 3 capable. These are called **Layer 3 switches** or **multilayer switches** (know both terms).

A multilayer switch can do both switching **and** routing:

- You can assign **IP addresses** to its interfaces, like a router.
- You can configure **routed ports** — physical interfaces that behave like router interfaces instead of switchports.
- You can create **SVIs** (Switch Virtual Interfaces) — virtual interfaces, one per VLAN, each with an IP address.
- You can configure **routes**, such as static routes, exactly like on a router.
- It can perform **inter-VLAN routing** without any router involved.

sections.title: The three methods of inter-VLAN routing

rows: One physical router interface and one cable per VLAN
Simple, but wastes interfaces — routers rarely have enough ports
One trunk link carrying all VLANs, with a router sub-interface per VLAN
Efficient on interfaces, but all inter-VLAN traffic goes to the router and back, which can congest the link in a busy network
SVIs on the switch route between VLANs locally
Preferred in large networks — traffic never leaves the switch

steps.narration: PC2 in VLAN 20 pings PC1 in VLAN 10. Its default gateway is no longer R1 — it is SW2's VLAN 20 SVI. The frame goes to SW2.
SW2 has its own routing table. It looks up 192.168.1.0/26 and finds it directly connected to the VLAN 10 SVI. The packet is routed into VLAN 10 — no router needed.
SW2 forwards the frame to SW1 over the trunk, tagged VLAN 10. (If the destination MAC were unknown, it would flood it out all VLAN 10 interfaces.)
SW1 delivers the frame to PC1. With ROAS this traffic would have made an extra round trip to R1 and back.
For destinations outside the LAN, SW2 uses its default route out of the routed port G0/1 to R1 — a plain point-to-point Layer 3 link, no VLANs on it.

sections.title: Configuring a routed port and SVIs

steps.narration: On R1, remove the old router-on-a-stick sub-interfaces.
Reset the physical interface to its default settings. (Deleted sub-interfaces still show as `deleted` in show ip interface brief until a reload — harmless.)
Give R1 its end of the new point-to-point /30 link.
On SW2, reset the port that used to be the ROAS trunk.
The command you must not forget. This enables Layer 3 routing so the switch can build its own routing table. Without it, inter-VLAN routing will not work.
Enter the interface facing R1.
Convert it from a Layer 2 switchport to a Layer 3 routed port. Now it can take an IP address.
Assign the switch's end of the /30 link.
Add a default route pointing at R1 so traffic leaving the LAN is sent there.
Create the SVI for VLAN 10. This is the PCs' new default gateway.
Same address R1 used for ROAS — the last usable address of the subnet — so no PC needs reconfiguring.
SVIs are shut down by default. Never forget this command.
Repeat for VLAN 20 and VLAN 30 the same way.
In the VLAN column, G0/1 now shows `routed` instead of a VLAN number.
The switch now has a real routing table — connected and local routes per SVI, plus the default route to R1.

sections.title: Four conditions for an SVI to be up/up

rows: The VLAN must exist on the switch
Unlike `switchport access vlan`, creating an SVI does NOT auto-create the VLAN
At least one up/up access port in the VLAN, and/or one up/up trunk port that allows the VLAN
A VLAN with no hosts can still come up if a trunk allows it
The VLAN itself must not be shut down
This is the VLAN, not the SVI — `vlan 10` then `shutdown` disables it
The SVI itself must not be shut down
SVIs are shut down by default, so `no shutdown` is required

content.body: Two commands are commonly confused. `ip routing` enables Layer 3 routing on the whole switch. `no switchport` converts one individual interface into a routed port so it can take an IP address. You need both for a Layer 3 switch uplink — and neither of them creates an SVI.

questions.question: Which TWO options are valid ways to configure the native VLAN on a router in a router-on-a-stick configuration? (Each is a complete solution.)
questions.explanation: You can either add the `native` keyword to `encapsulation dot1q` on the sub-interface, or skip the sub-interface entirely and configure the native VLAN's IP address on the physical interface — in which case `encapsulation dot1q` is not needed.

options.label: B
options.text: `interface g0/0.10` then `encapsulation dot1q 10 native` then `ip address ...`

options.label: C
options.text: `interface g0/0` then `ip address ...` (no sub-interface, no encapsulation command)

questions.question: You create an SVI for VLAN 225 on SW1, assign an IP address and issue `no shutdown`, but the interface stays down/down. Which TWO options might be the cause?
questions.explanation: An SVI needs the VLAN to exist on the switch, and needs at least one up/up access port in that VLAN or an up/up trunk allowing it. `switchport` commands are not valid on an SVI at all.

options.label: A
options.text: VLAN 225 does not exist on the switch

options.label: B
options.text: You didn't issue `switchport mode trunk` on the SVI

options.label: C
options.text: You didn't issue `switchport access vlan 225` on the SVI

options.label: D
options.text: No interfaces in VLAN 225 are up/up

questions.question: Which command configures a switch interface as a routed port?
questions.explanation: `no switchport` turns the interface from a Layer 2 switchport into a Layer 3 routed port, allowing an IP address to be assigned. `ip routing` enables routing on the switch as a whole, but does not change an individual interface.

questions.question: On a Catalyst switch you issue: `interface fa0/7`, `switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q`, `switchport mode trunk`, `switchport trunk native vlan 44`. What is true of VLAN traffic sent over Fa0/7?
questions.explanation: Traffic in the native VLAN is sent untagged over a trunk. The native VLAN was changed to 44, so VLAN 44 traffic is untagged. By default it would have been VLAN 1.

options.label: C
options.text: All VLAN traffic will be tagged

options.label: D
options.text: All VLAN traffic will be untagged

questions.question: In a Wireshark capture of a tagged frame, which value identifies it as 802.1Q tagged?
questions.explanation: The TPID field, located where the Type field normally sits (right after the source MAC), always carries 0x8100 to mark the frame as 802.1Q tagged.

options.label: C
options.text: A VLAN ID of 1 in the VID field

questions.question: Why is a multilayer switch preferred over router on a stick in large networks?
questions.explanation: With ROAS every inter-VLAN packet travels to the router and back over the same link, which can congest it. A multilayer switch routes between VLANs internally using SVIs.

options.label: B
options.text: It avoids sending all inter-VLAN traffic to the router and back over one link

options.label: C
options.text: It does not require 802.1Q tagging anywhere in the network
